reconcile.connective: The Geneva Bible's annotators read Luke 1:6 as displaying the fruit of righteousness, not its ground, which they locate in faith alone.

discrepancy.connective: Heikki Räisänen presses the sharpest version: Paul's statements on the law, including Romans 2:13, are not harmonizable but reflect genuine, unresolved inconsistency.

skeptic.name: Heikki Räisänen
skeptic.attribution: Heikki Räisänen, Paul and the Law, WUNT 29 (Tübingen: J.C.B. Mohr [Paul Siebeck], 1983)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Whom no man could justly reprove: now so it is, that the fruits of justification are set forth here, and not the cause, which is faith only, and nothing else.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers whether Luke 1:6's righteousness-language makes law-keeping the ground of justification: the annotators say law-walking is the fruit/evidence, faith alone is the cause -- the same distinction Reformed exegesis applies to Romans 2:13 and Galatians 2:21.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under 'Doctrinal Discrepancies,' Haley's parallel 'Justification: By Faith / By Works' table places Romans 2:13 ("the doers of the law shall be justified") directly opposite Romans 3:20, Galatians 2:16, and Galatians 3:11-12, then argues works are the fruit of faith rather than its antecedent ground, so the two columns 'affirm the inseparable connection...of faith and works as cause and effect' (pp. 167-168).

link.title: CARM: Does Romans 2:13 mean that we are justified before God by keeping the Law?
link.note: live apologetic treatment arguing Romans 2:13 does not make law-keeping a condition of justification
